context: Al-Layl came down in Makkah in the early years of the message, in the same season as its sister oath-surahs, when revelation still arrived as short bursts of rhythm meant to be carried in the memory of a small, pressured community. Makkah at that hour was a city where wealth decided worth: a man was measured by what he held, and the poor believer was treated as proof against his own religion. Into that market logic the surah dropped a different accounting, two hands moving in two directions, one giving and one gripping, and two roads being smoothed under two kinds of feet.

Classical commentators, Ibn Kathir among them, record that many early authorities read its closing verses in the light of Abu Bakr, who spent his wealth buying tortured slaves like Bilal out of their chains, seeking no favor and expecting no repayment, only the face of his Lord Most High. Whether or not one insists on that occasion, the surah lived in the community as its portrait of the purified giver. The Prophet ﷺ also named it among the surahs an imam should choose when leading people, short enough for the weak, deep enough for anyone.
name_story: The surah is named for its first oath, wal-layli idha yaghsha, by the night when it covers over. In the hadith collections and the earliest codices it is simply Al-Layl, The Night, cited by its opening words. No other name is soundly attached to it.

movements.note: Night, day, and the creation of male and female are called as witnesses to one verdict: human striving runs in opposite directions, and no two lives are spending themselves on the same thing.

The one who gives, guards himself, and trusts the best promise is eased toward ease; the one who hoards, feels self-sufficient, and calls the promise a lie is eased toward hardship, and his wealth will not descend the cliff with him.
Guidance is Allah’s to give, the last life and the first are His, and the blazing fire ahead is entered only by the most wretched, the one who denied and turned away.

The god-fearing one who gives his wealth to be purified, owing no one and collecting from no one, wanting only the face of his Lord Most High, is promised the last word of the surah: he will be satisfied.

themes.d: The surah reduces every biography to the motion of a hand. Generosity joined to faith is one road; hoarding joined to denial is the other, and each road runs downhill in its own direction.
Allah does not only judge the traveler, He smooths the road the traveler chose. Fa-sanuyassiruhu, We will ease him: obedience becomes lighter with practice, and so does refusal.
At the moment of falling, ma yughni anhu maluhu, his wealth avails him nothing. The surah lets money keep every power except the one that matters.
The praised giver takes no repayment and settles no debts of favor. His giving has one address, the face of his Lord, which is why it purifies him instead of purchasing people.

heart: Recited slowly, Al-Layl performs a quiet audit. It does not ask what you believe; it asks which way your hand was moving this week. The frightening mercy of the surah is verse seven and verse ten said together: whichever direction you lean, heaven greases the slope. Every generous act is making the next one easier, and every refusal is doing the same. A person reading this at night begins to feel his habits not as isolated choices but as a road being paved under him while he walks, and he checks, urgently, where the road is pointed.

Then the ending turns the audit into a promise. Wa lasawfa yarda, and he will surely be satisfied: the giver who wanted only His face is not told he will be rich or safe, he is told he will be content, which is the thing the hoarder was buying all along and never received. The surah closes by handing the poorest sincere giver the only prize the wealthy denier ever wanted.

passages.why: Stop on the promise that obedience is made easy for the one who begins it, and feel how mercy works on the road itself.
One verse ends the oldest illusion: wealth stays at the top of the cliff when its owner goes over.
The purest sentence of motive in the Quran: giving only to seek the face of his Lord, the Most High.
The surah’s last word, satisfaction, is the wage no market in Makkah could price.

connections.why: The night of this surah gives way to the morning brightness of the next, and the mushaf itself moves from the two roads to the consoled traveler on the best of them.
Al-Insan shows the same motive in action, those who feed the poor saying they want only the face of Allah, no repayment and no thanks.

virtue.text: When Mu’adh lengthened the prayer, the Prophet ﷺ told him to lead people instead with short luminous surahs and named this one among them, so Al-Layl carries his ﷺ own recommendation as a surah for congregational prayer.
